beats.title: THE CRASH
beats.narration_text: A battery can be most of the way full and still be finished for the thing it powers. The gadget resets, the screen goes dark, and the cell can still have plenty inside. So what, exactly, ran out? In that case, it was not the charge.

beats.title: THE SETUP
beats.narration_text: I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. I did not open a real battery. I built a model of a C R twenty thirty-two coin cell from two manufacturers' published graphs. Then I asked it one question again and again: how much is still left at the moment a device resets?
beats.visual_intent: Tank and chart stay. Two source chips slide in at the side, each held 2 s or more: 'Duracell CR2032 datasheet: 3.0 V, 225 mAh' and 'Energizer coin handbook p.4: resistance curve (read by me, about)'. A third chip: 'model: my code, seed 32'. The question is written once: how much is left when the device resets?
beats.status: PUBLIC (Duracell, Energizer sheets; FACTCHECK 1,2) + OUR OWN model

beats.title: THE HIDDEN RESISTOR
beats.narration_text: First, why a battery's voltage drops at all. A coin cell is a three volt source with a small resistor hidden inside it. Energizer, a maker of these cells, says a fresh one starts near ten ohms. When a device asks for current, some of the voltage is spent pushing that current through the resistor, and what is left is what the device sees. Ask for thirty milliamps, and a fresh cell loses about three tenths of a volt. Voltage at the terminals equals the open voltage, minus the current times the resistance.
beats.visual_intent: The chart dims. A cell drawn as a 3 V source with a small resistor inside a box, labelled 'about 10 ohm, fresh (Energizer handbook p.4)' and '3.0 V open-circuit (Duracell datasheet)'. A device arrow draws 30 mA; a voltmeter at the terminals reads 3.0 V open, then 2.7 V under load. The sum is written beside it: 0.030 A x 10 ohm = 0.3 V. The line 'terminal voltage = open voltage - current x resistance' is held 2 s or more.
beats.status: PUBLIC (Energizer p.4: starts near 10 ohm; 3 V nominal) + OUR OWN arithmetic

beats.title: THE LINE
beats.narration_text: Now give the device a reset line. Below some voltage, it restarts. I chose two volts for mine. That turns into a limit. The largest burst the cell can pass is the open voltage, minus two volts, divided by the resistance. A fresh cell, at ten ohms, can pass about a hundred milliamps. Anything larger, and the device resets on the first try. So there is a line, and your burst either sits under it or it does not.
beats.visual_intent: A voltmeter strip with a red line at 2.0 V labelled 'reset line: my choice'. The chart returns; only the fresh point of THE LINE is plotted at x = 0, y = 100 mA, with a short stub (the rest of the line is drawn in B04, so it never looks flat). Formula card: biggest burst = (open voltage - reset voltage) / resistance; fresh: (3.0 - 2.0) / 10 ohm = 100 mA. Labels beside the stub: above the line RESET, below the line runs. A burst drawn above the point flashes RESET.
beats.status: OUR OWN (chosen 2.0 V reset line; arithmetic)

beats.title: THE LINE MOVES
beats.narration_text: Here is what made me sit up. The resistor does not stay ten ohms. Energizer's own plot, from a pulse test of about thirty milliamps, shows it climbing as the cell is used. As I read it: about fourteen ohms, then nineteen, then twenty-eight, then forty-five, and about sixty-five at the very end. So the line comes down. At the start, about a hundred milliamps. A hundred and fifty milliamp-hours in, about forty-three. Near the end, about eight and a half. The cell is the same cell the whole time. What it can safely give is not.
beats.visual_intent: THE LINE draws left to right and falls as the tank drains: 100 mA at 0, 69 at 25 mAh, 63 at 100, 43 at 150, 26 at 185, 14 at 200, 8.5 at 208. Beneath it, a resistance strip drawn by us (not the maker's graph): 10, 14, 19, 28, 45, about 65 ohm, labelled 'my reading of Energizer p.4, ~30 mA pulse test'. The line and the strip are side by side, held 2 s or more. Callouts at 150 mAh (43 mA) and at the end (8.5 mA).
beats.status: PUBLIC (Energizer p.4 plot, 75 ohm / ~30 mA pulse) read by me, 'about' + OUR OWN model

beats.title: A SMALL ASK
beats.narration_text: Now I make three asks. First, a small one: eight milliamps. I ran it all the way down. It never crosses the line. Even at the very end of the plotted run, the line is only just above eight. So in my model the device uses the whole cell, and nothing is stranded. At ten milliamps, the cell is nearly spent when it resets, with about one percent left. A small ask spends almost everything.
beats.visual_intent: An 8 mA ask is drawn as a horizontal line across the chart, below THE LINE all the way; the tank drains to empty. At the right end a magnified gap shows 8.5 against 8 ('only just above'). Readout: '8 mA: nothing left behind (my model)'. A 10 mA ask: crossing near 205 mAh, readout '10 mA: about 1% left'.

beats.title: A MEDIUM ASK
beats.narration_text: Second, a medium ask: thirty milliamps. Now the falling line meets it. It happens at about one hundred seventy-four milliamp-hours used, out of a plotted two hundred eight. The device resets with about sixteen and a half percent of the cell unspent. Roughly one part in six, locked inside a cell that tests fine.
beats.visual_intent: A 30 mA ask line. The falling line meets it at about 174 mAh; RESET flashes; the tank holds 16.5% (34 of 208 mAh), shaded. Readout: '30 mA: resets at 174 of 208 mAh used; 16.5% left (my model)'.

beats.title: A LARGE ASK
beats.narration_text: Third, a large ask: sixty milliamps. This one meets the line at about one hundred eight milliamp-hours. The device resets with almost half the cell unspent, forty-eight percent. And at a hundred milliamps, a fresh cell resets on the first burst, with all of it left. Same cell, three asks, and three different endings.
beats.visual_intent: A 60 mA ask line meets THE LINE at about 108 mAh; the tank shows 48% unspent. Then a 100 mA ask at x = 0 (fresh cell resets at once, tank full). The endings are held together, side by side, 2 s or more, headed 'three asks, plus the 100 mA extreme': 8 mA: 0%, 30 mA: 16.5%, 60 mA: 48%, 100 mA: 100% left behind.

beats.title: THE RULE
beats.narration_text: Here is the rule, and you can do it on paper. The largest burst a cell can pass is the open voltage, minus the reset voltage, divided by the resistance. Let's try one together, with an old cell: its resistance is forty ohms, and its open voltage is two point seven volts. Two point seven, minus two, is point seven. Point seven, divided by forty, is about seventeen and a half milliamps. Any burst over that, and the device resets, however much charge is left. Check it: a device asking for twenty-five milliamps resets on that old cell, and one asking for ten does not. Now do yours, by looking up two numbers in your device's data sheet: its biggest current draw, and the voltage where its chip resets.
beats.visual_intent: The rule card fills the frame: biggest burst = (open V - reset V) / resistance. A worked line builds step by step: old cell, 40 ohm, 2.7 V: 2.7 - 2.0 = 0.7; 0.7 / 40 = about 17.5 mA. Two check chips: '25 mA: RESET', '10 mA: runs'. Two blank fields for the viewer: 'my device's biggest draw: ___ mA' and 'my chip's reset voltage: ___ V', plus 'look in the data sheet'. Each step held 2 s or more.
beats.status: OUR OWN (arithmetic on the signed rule)

beats.title: WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER
beats.narration_text: I pushed on the model to see what moves it. Raise the reset line from two volts to two point four, and the thirty milliamp ask strands forty-two percent, not sixteen and a half. Energizer's handbook makes the same point: a device whose cutoff is above two volts may leave significant capacity unused. Use a resistance curve from a very slow drain, and the same ask strands about forty percent. And one cell is not every cell. If I let resistance vary by about fifteen percent from cell to cell, most cells at thirty milliamps land between about eleven and twenty-three percent.
beats.visual_intent: Three panels in turn, each held 2 s or more, each repeating the 30 mA ask: (1) reset line 2.4 V: 42% left behind, beside the base 16.5%; (2) a quote chip from the Energizer handbook, p.2: 'may leave significant capacity unused'; (3) a slow-drain resistance curve (Energizer p.4 inset, my reading): about 40% left behind. Last, a band 11% to 23% with 'resistance varied about 15% cell to cell: my assumption'.
beats.status: OUR OWN (stranded_energy.py sensitivity) + PUBLIC (Energizer handbook p.2 quote)

beats.title: WHAT THIS IS NOT
beats.narration_text: Let me be plain about what this is. It is a model, fitted to graphs I read off two data sheets, so every number is about, not exact. I tested no real cell. I did not model cold, which makes the voltage drop worse. I did not model a capacitor. And the reset line is my own choice, not a chip's. What holds is the shape: the bigger the ask, the more is left behind.
beats.visual_intent: A ledger of what was not done, items appearing one by one on the same chart: 'a model, graphs read by me: every number is about'; 'no real cell tested'; 'no cold'; 'no capacitor'; 'the reset line is my choice (2.0 V)'. Last line in a different weight: 'holds: the bigger the ask, the more is left behind'.

on_screen.text: ledger: reset line 2.0 V is my choice

beats.title: YOUR TURN
beats.narration_text: So the next time something resets with a battery that still reads fine, do not ask how much charge is left. Ask how big its biggest burst is, and where the line sits. A cell can die rich. How rich depends on what you ask of it.
beats.visual_intent: The scene returns to its frame-one structure with the three asks (8, 30, 60 mA) marked on the chart and the tank full. Text: 'how rich depends on what you ask'. The two blanks from B08 return. End card: 'The Cell Dies Rich'. Nothing else new.
